new_cases.source_claim: Every track in Live can host a number of devices. These devices can be of three different sorts: MIDI effects act upon MIDI signals and can only be placed in MIDI tracks. Audio effects act upon audio signals and can be placed in audio tracks, return tracks, and the Main track. They can also be added to MIDI tracks as long as they are placed after an instrument. Live’s devices can be accessed in the browser. The browser’s sidebar contains labels for built-in devices, Max for Live devices, and third-party plug-ins. The easiest way to place a device in a track is to double-click it in the browser, which adds it to the selected track or creates a new track if one is not selected. Alternatively, select a destination track by clicking within it, then select a device or preset in the browser and press Enter to add it to the selected track. You can also drag devices into tracks or drop areas in the Session and Arrangement Views, or into the Device View. Dragging a sample to the Device View of a MIDI track creates a Simpler instrument with this sample loaded. To add another device to the track, simply drag it there or double-click its name to append it to the device chain. Signals in a device chain always travel from left to right. You can drop audio effects in at any point in an audio track’s device chain, keeping in mind that the order of effects determines the resulting sound. The same is true for a MIDI track’s device chain.

new_cases.source_claim: Every built-in Live device includes two device states, A and B, which can store separate parameter values. This lets you save and compare the changes you make when creating or editing presets. You can save an iteration of a preset that you don’t want to overwrite to one device state and continue experimenting on the other. When a device is first loaded, its default parameter values are used for both A and B. Once you adjust a parameter, B retains the initial values, and any changes you make only apply to A. To copy the current parameter values from the A device state to B, select the Compare: Copy A to B command from the Edit menu, the device’s context menu, or its Show Options toggle. You can switch from the A device state to B using the Compare: Switch to B command or the P key. When the B device state is selected, a “(B)” appears next to the device’s name in the title bar. The Compare commands are available for both device states, so how you save parameter values to A and B is up to you. You could use one device state to keep the default values as a reference, or use both states to design completely different-sounding presets. Note that these commands are not available for Racks, Max for Live devices, or plug-ins.

new_cases.source_claim: Because A and B are unique device states, any parameter automation you create in one state is not shared with the other. This means if you automate a parameter in the A device state, that automation will be disabled when you switch to B and is not automatically re-enabled when you switch back to A. To reactivate any disabled parameter automation, use the Re-Enable Automation command in the parameter’s context menu when the device state you want to use is selected. This command can be used from either device state. Keep in mind that since automation is specific to A and B, it will be disabled again each time you switch from one state to the other.

new_cases.source_claim: Live devices can store and retrieve their parameter settings as presets. Each device appears in the content pane of the browser as a folder that can be opened to reveal its presets. The folder represents the default preset for a device; this can be either the original factory settings or a custom default you have saved. The presets within the folder have custom settings. Presets are included as part of the Core Library and Packs. You can also create and save your own presets. You can browse and load presets quickly with the computer keyboard: Scroll up and down using the up and down arrow keys. Close and open device folders using the left and right arrow keys. You can also double-click a preset in the browser to load it onto a selected track, or drag and drop a preset from the browser onto a track’s title bar or device chain. Note that it is generally recommended to load presets via the browser; however, it is also possible to drag Live-specific device file types (such as .adg, .adv, and .amxd) directly into a Live Set from the Explorer (Win) / Finder (Mac). If you want to replace a preset on a track with a different one, you can drag and drop a new preset from the browser and place it over the existing preset in the track’s device chain.

new_cases.source_claim: Using Hot-Swap mode is a quick way to replace a preset on a track. In this mode, the preset on the track is linked to the browser so that you can audition and load different presets. To start hot-swapping, press Q or click the Hot-Swap Presets button in the device’s title bar. If you press Q to enter Hot-Swap mode, the currently selected preset on the track will be made available for swapping. If no preset is selected, the first audio effect (on audio tracks) or the instrument (on MIDI tracks) will be swapped. Once Hot-Swap mode is enabled, the preset is selected in the browser and its device folder is expanded. You can replace the preset with another one from the same folder or navigate to a different folder to swap in a preset for another device. Only presets of the same device type can be hot-swapped. For example, it is not possible to swap an audio effect for a MIDI effect. Use the up and down arrow keys to navigate through the presets. Press Enter to load the selected preset or double-click the preset you want to load. If you want to use a device’s default settings, select the device’s parent folder and load that instead of one of its presets. Once you are done replacing presets, you can exit Hot-Swap mode with any of the following actions: Press the Q key. Click the X button in the Hot-Swap bar at the top of the browser’s content pane. Click the X button in the device’s title bar. Navigate from the browser to a different view.

new_cases.source_claim: The controls in a device’s title bar can be used to activate or deactivate the device, save and hot-swap presets, create defaults, and open the device’s context menu. You can create custom defaults to save and apply the settings you use the most for certain devices and workflows. Defaults allow you to: Load devices with pre-defined parameter values. All defaults are stored in the Defaults folder in the User Library. Once a default is saved, its settings are automatically applied whenever it is used in a Set. To remove a saved default, use the Delete option from its context menu in the User Library, or select the item in the browser and press the Delete key. Once removed, the factory settings are once again applied for the corresponding item. Each Live device loads with its factory settings when added to a track. You can save a device with a set of specified parameter values as a default preset so that the device loads with those settings instead. To do so, set the desired parameter values for a device, then select the Save as Default Preset option from the device title bar’s Options menu or context menu. This option is available for all of Live’s instruments, MIDI effects, audio effects, and Rack types. After the option is selected, the device is saved to the relevant folder within the Defaults folder: Audio Effects, Instruments, or MIDI Effects. You can also drag the device from a track into one of the device type folders to save it as a default preset. Make sure the preset has the original device name (e.g., Simpler) and not a unique name; otherwise, the preset will not be recognized as a default. Once the preset is saved, its settings are loaded any time you add the device to a track. If you save a default for an instrument that contains a sample, the sample is also loaded. If you create a new default for a device that already has one, a dialog appears asking if you want to overwrite the existing preset.

new_cases.source_claim: Load VST and Audio Units plug-ins with specific parameter configurations. You can save the parameter configuration for a VST or Audio Units plug-in as a default. Add the parameters you want to include in Configure Mode, then select the Save as Default Configuration option in the device title bar’s Options menu or context menu. The default is saved to its respective folder, either Audio Units or VSTs, in the Plug-In Configurations folder, which is automatically created the first time you save a default configuration. new_cases.source_claim: Customize the presets used for sample dropping, slicing, and converting audio to MIDI. Similar to slicing presets, you can set up custom Racks for converting Harmony, Melody, or Drums to MIDI. It is recommended to use an Instrument Rack for the Harmony and Melody conversions, that way you can add MIDI and audio effects to the device chain. However, it is also possible to use a single instrument on its own if desired. The Drums to MIDI conversion requires a Drum Rack with Sampler or Simpler devices on its pads. Add the devices you want to use to the Instrument Rack (if using one), or add the drum hits you want included in the Drum Rack. Adjust the device parameters and map them to the Macro Controls as needed. Drag the configured device or Rack into one of the three Audio to MIDI folders: Drums to MIDI, Harmony to MIDI, or Melody to MIDI to save it as a default. You can also drag an existing device or Rack preset into the conversion folders instead of creating one from scratch. Make sure to only add a Drum Rack to the Drums to MIDI folder, and not a Drum Rack nested in an Instrument Rack; otherwise, the preset will not be recognized as a default. After the default is saved, it will be used any time you run its corresponding conversion command. Note that while it is possible to add multiple presets to the same conversion folder, only one default can be used at a time. When running the conversion command, the preset that was last added to the folder is used.

new_cases.source_claim: In addition to creating program-wide defaults, you can also save Project-specific ones. This can be useful if you need specialized device or workflow settings for a particular Set but don’t want to overwrite the more general defaults you use on a regular basis. To store Project-specific defaults, add a separate Defaults folder to the Current Project folder, along with any of its related folders that you want to use. You can create these folders directly in the Project folder in Explorer (Win) or Finder (Mac), or use the New Folder context menu option for the Current Project in the browser. Once created, you can drag custom devices or tracks into their corresponding folders. It is not possible to drag a plug-in into the Current Project folder, so there is a workaround for saving Project-specific plug-in configurations. Make sure to first create the Plug-In Configurations, Audio Units, and VSTs folders in the Defaults folder for the Current Project. You can then save a configuration as normal and drag the plug-in folder with the Default.appc file from the User Library into the Audio Units or VSTs folder in the Current Project. Since this removes the configuration from the main Defaults folder, you can save the same default again if you also want a copy in the User Library, or create a new one with different settings. Once the Project-specific defaults are set up, they will be loaded instead of the ones from the Defaults folder in the User Library any time you use their corresponding items in a Set from the Project. Note that the context menu options for saving defaults are specifically for storing presets in the Defaults folder in the User Library, and therefore cannot be used to save Project-specific defaults.
